first_impression.reaction: My fiancee wants to skip the seating chart, I think it's a recipe for chaos, so I Googled it to settle it. Jumped to the FAQ first. Short, straight answers, no fluff, so I went back up. The intro doesn't pretend open seating is all upside: it names the aunt with the plate straight away, which is the exact argument I was going to make. The three-question test is useful and the allergen and accessibility bits are sourced to FSANZ and the Queensland Government, which I can actually check. Where it loses me is the same place as every planner site: three Wedded Concierge pitches, and the only thing I learn about the fee is that it exists and gets agreed in writing. Nothing on how it's calculated or whether you take a cut from the venue or caterer.

journey.quote: Yes. It suits cocktail receptions, shared or station dinners, small weddings and guest lists who know each other. Reserve seats for family and elders, set extra chairs and tell guests in advance.
journey.reaction: Direct answer, then the conditions. That's what I want from an FAQ. Gave me enough to keep reading the rest.

journey.quote: It depends on the room, the table shapes and how your guests group together. Ask your venue how many extra seats to set for your layout, and where spare chairs can be kept close by.
journey.reaction: No number. I'd have liked a rule of thumb, but I'd rather 'ask the venue' than a made-up percentage. I'll live with it.

journey.quote: It can work beautifully. It can also leave an elderly aunt hovering with a plate while younger guests claim the good tables.
journey.reaction: 'Beautifully' is the kind of word I skip, but the second sentence earns it back. Honest about the downside from line two.

journey.section: Do you need a seating chart for a wedding?
journey.quote: Ask yourself three questions. Will guests be served a plated meal at a set time? Is the guest list made up of groups who don't know each other? Do some family members need to be seated with care?
journey.reaction: A decision rule, not vibes. We answer yes to at least two of these, so that settles our argument in about ten seconds.

journey.section: When skipping the seating chart backfires
journey.quote: If guests chose their main course with their RSVP, the kitchen needs to know where each guest sits. Without a plan, waiters ask every guest what they ordered, and service slows for the whole room.
journey.reaction: Practical, operational reason. This is the bit I'll show my fiancee.

journey.section: Guests with allergies and dietary needs
journey.quote: That obligation sits with your caterer, not with you, and this isn't legal advice.
journey.reaction: Good. Sourced to FSANZ, then clear about where the responsibility sits and that it's not legal advice. That's the kind of limitation I trust.

journey.quote: The same guidance advises against seating everyone who uses a wheelchair together.
journey.reaction: Didn't know that, and it's attributed to an actual Queensland Government guide I can open. Wouldn't have thought of it.

journey.section: Give your caterer a plan for dietary meals
journey.quote: When food isn't packaged or labelled, allergen information must be displayed with the food or can be requested from the supplier.
journey.reaction: Already told me this further up. Second time round it reads like padding.

journey.section: Give your caterer a plan for dietary meals
journey.quote: If you are organising all of this from another country, Wedded Concierge brings the venue, travel and vendors into one plan.
journey.reaction: First pitch, dropped into the middle of an allergy section. Doesn't follow from anything above it. 'Brings the vendors into one plan': and does the planner get paid by those vendors?

journey.section: Open seating at a destination wedding across several days
journey.quote: Let the welcome dinner be open. Guests from different cities meet over long shared tables, and by the wedding dinner the strangers have become friends.
journey.reaction: That's a promise, not a fact. Some of them will still be strangers. The advice (open welcome dinner, light plan for the main dinner) is fine on its own.

journey.section: Open seating at a destination wedding across several days
journey.quote: Does the catering team need table numbers or a seating plan for plated service?
journey.reaction: Useful list of questions for the venue. Straight into the spreadsheet.

journey.section: Open seating at a destination wedding across several days
journey.quote: Through Wedded Concierge, one Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you from start to finish as your single point of contact, works in your time zone and confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Second pitch. 'Inclusions in writing' is the right instinct, but I still don't know what's included in your own fee, or whether seating plans and caterer liaison are part of it or an extra.

journey.section: Planning the rest of the weekend
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor quotes in AUD for Australian couples and agrees the fee with you in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Better than nothing: there's a fee and it's in writing. But how much, how it's worked out, and do you take a cut from the venue or caterer on top? This article tells me to brief the caterer in detail and ask the venue everything. Same standard should apply to you.

unanswered_questions: Do you take a commission or mark-up from the venue, caterer or other vendors you bring 'into one plan'? (deferred business detail)
How is the Wedded Wonderland fee calculated, and what's a realistic 'From AUD' figure? (deferred business detail)
Is building the seating plan, briefing the caterer on dietary meals and liaising with the venue coordinator included in the Wedded Advisor's fee, or charged as an extra? (deferred business detail)
Show me a real wedding you've planned that used open seating or reserved tables, with how it went and the actual budget. (deferred business detail)
Is there any rule of thumb for how many extra seats to set, or does it genuinely vary too much to say?

turn_offs_found.quote: If you are organising all of this from another country, Wedded Concierge brings the venue, travel and vendors into one plan.
turn_offs_found.why: Pitch wedged into a sourced allergy section with no link to what came before, and it raises the vendor-commission question without answering it.

turn_offs_found.quote: Let the welcome dinner be open. Guests from different cities meet over long shared tables, and by the wedding dinner the strangers have become friends.
turn_offs_found.why: Emotional promise presented as an outcome. Nothing backs it up.

turn_offs_found.quote: Your Wedded Advisor quotes in AUD for Australian couples and agrees the fee with you in writing before any work begins.
turn_offs_found.why: The fee is mentioned at the point I'm asked to enquire, but not how it works or whether suppliers pay you too. That's my main question about any planner.

would_share_with: My fiancee: the three-question test under 'Do you need a seating chart for a wedding?' and the plated-meal point, to settle our argument
Our Reddit thread: the Queensland Government accessible events guidance on reserved seating and not grouping wheelchair users together

cta_reaction.quote: Start a conversation through Wedded Concierge, and for more planning ideas, read the Wedded Wonderland magazine.
cta_reaction.why: Useful, honest, sourced article and it answered what I came for. But I came for a seating question, not a planner, and three pitches in I still don't know what the planner costs, what's in the fee, or whether you take a cut from the venue or caterer. I'd keep comparing.

top_3_changes: Move or cut the mid-article pitch in 'Give your caterer a plan for dietary meals'; it breaks a sourced section and makes the brand look like it's selling before it's finished helping.

Drop the repeated allergen declaration sentence in the dietary meals section (it restates the earlier FSANZ point) and tone down 'by the wedding dinner the strangers have become friends' to something you can stand behind.

At the closing CTA, say how the Wedded Wonderland fee works, whether supplier commissions or mark-ups apply, and whether seating and caterer liaison are included (deferred business detail), so the brand meets the 'confirm it in writing' standard the article sets for venues and caterers.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection
Stayed in character as Daniel (sceptic): FAQ first, checked sources and claims, hunted for fees and commissions
No invented brand facts; fees, commissions, inclusions and real weddings listed as deferred unanswered questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots) ignored
Did not invent problems; low-severity points kept low and positives recorded where earned

open_questions.question: The allergen declaration point appears twice (Guests with allergies section and dietary meals section, both FSANZ). Should the second be trimmed to the practical caterer advice only?

assumptions: Daniel arrived via a Google search for 'wedding without seating chart' to settle a disagreement with his fiancee, while also comparing planners.
Business details (fees, commissions, inclusions, real weddings) are deferred; voiced as unanswered questions only.
Link text quoted as rendered, without markdown syntax or HTML comments.
Read FAQ first, then the intro, decision test, backfire and dietary sections and destination section closely; the 'what to do instead' layout options skimmed.
